headline: Artificial Intelligence Proves Longtime Math Rule on Quantum Computers

sentences.text: Two scientists asked a hard question about fast future computers.
Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis wrote their idea in 2011.
They thought normal computers can solve some problems as fast.
An artificial intelligence program found the real answer later.
David Turturean used Fable 5.2 to complete the full proof.

grammar.title: Modal Verb Can
grammar.note: The modal auxiliary 'can' expresses ability or possibility. Here, it indicates that regular computers have the capability to solve certain problems at equal speed.

grammar.title: To-Infinitive of Purpose
grammar.note: An infinitive phrase starting with 'to' can express why an action was performed. In this sentence, it explains the purpose behind using Fable 5.2.

sentences.text: In 2011, two scientists shared an idea about future fast computers.
Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis thought standard machines could match them.
They focused on simple questions with random strings of zeros and ones.
David Turturean worked with a new program named Fable 5.2.
The software tested the idea and finished the full check in four days.
This clear result will help experts design better tests in the future.

grammar.title: Past Participle Modifier
grammar.note: The past participle 'named' forms a phrase describing the noun 'program'. It functions like an adjective phrase to provide a specific title for the software.

grammar.title: Help + Object + Bare Infinitive
grammar.note: The verb 'help' allows a direct object followed by a base verb without 'to'. Here, 'experts' is the object and 'design' is the bare infinitive showing what they are assisted to do.

sentences.text: Researchers have finally confirmed a long-standing limit for advanced quantum computers.
In 2011, Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis proposed a math conjecture about random bit strings.
A conjecture is a mathematical guess that needs a formal proof.
They suggested that traditional hardware can match quantum speed on completely random data problems.
David Turturean and his team at Physical Superintelligence recently tested this famous guess.
An artificial intelligence system called Fable 5.2 completed the logical proof in four days.
Researchers at Stanford University have reviewed the output to explain how the proof works.

grammar.title: Present Perfect Tense
grammar.note: The present perfect structure ('have confirmed') connects a past action to the present moment. The adverb 'finally' is placed between the auxiliary and main verb to show completion after a long time.

grammar.title: Relative Clause with That
grammar.note: The relative pronoun 'that' introduces a clause defining the noun 'guess'. It acts as the subject of the verb 'needs' within the subordinate clause.

grammar.title: Embedded Question
grammar.note: An indirect question can function as a noun phrase within a sentence. Notice that it maintains standard statement word order: subject ('the proof') followed by verb ('works').

sentences.text: A long-standing mathematical conjecture regarding the limits of quantum computers has been proven using artificial intelligence.
In 2011, computer scientists Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis suggested quantum devices lacked major advantages for random tasks.
Their hypothesis proposed that conventional computers could match quantum performance when evaluating random strings of binary bits.
David Turturean from the company Physical Superintelligence tackled the problem by using Anthropic's Fable 5.2 model.
The software spent four days writing the proof and validating its steps with checking tools named Lean.
Researchers at Stanford University analyzed the AI output and reported that the proof was entirely original.
Mathematician Shachar Lovett noted that these new automated tools would allow researchers to pursue more ambitious questions.
Experts emphasized that quantum speedups remain likely for structured problems, such as simulating complex industrial molecules.

grammar.title: Present Perfect Passive
grammar.note: This passive verb structure combines 'has been' with the past participle 'proven'. It puts focus on the conjecture being resolved rather than explicitly stating the agent first.

grammar.title: Reduced Adverbial Clause
grammar.note: The conjunction 'when' introduces an abbreviated clause where the subject and verb are omitted ('when they are evaluating'). This makes the sentence more concise while retaining clear temporal meaning.

grammar.title: Allow + Object + To-Infinitive
grammar.note: The verb 'allow' takes a direct object ('researchers') followed by an infinitive phrase ('to pursue...'). This pattern expresses enabling someone to carry out an action.

sentences.text: Artificial intelligence has formally resolved a decades-old mathematical conjecture that defines the computational limits of quantum computers.
In 2011, computer scientists Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis posited that quantum systems lack major advantages when processing unstructured, random data.
Their proposal questioned whether quantum algorithms could process random bit strings significantly faster than standard computers taking basic queries.
David Turturean and his colleagues at Physical Superintelligence revisited the unsolved problem by deploying Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 model.
Over four days, the system generated the mathematical proof, refined its logic, and successfully validated the results with Lean software.
Stanford researchers Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle, and Li-Yang Tan examined the AI output and published an explanatory paper.
Mathematician Shachar Lovett observed that the logical techniques uncovered by the AI offer valuable strategies for future mathematical research.
While this finding narrows where quantum speedups apply, experts note that quantum hardware remains promising for structured tasks like simulating molecules.
Company representative Matthew Pines stated that his team now plans to use artificial intelligence to explore entirely new mathematical concepts.

grammar.title: Noun Clause with Whether
grammar.note: The subordinator 'whether' introduces a noun clause acting as the direct object of 'questioned'. It presents an indirect yes-no question regarding possibility.

grammar.title: Reduced Relative Clause
grammar.note: This past participle phrase replaces a full relative clause like 'that were uncovered by the AI'. It modifies the noun phrase 'the logical techniques' efficiently.

grammar.focus: While this finding narrows where quantum speedups apply,
grammar.title: Concession Clause with While
grammar.note: The conjunction 'while' introduces a dependent clause expressing concession or contrast. It sets up a qualification before presenting the main assertion about quantum hardware.
